To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the knowledge obtained from interpersonal networks in more developed countries is more useful to less developed country firms when it is novel, accessible and not too costly to obtain, and 2) the knowledge obtained through interpersonal networks in less developed countries is more valuable when it is not novel, accessible and when it is not too costly to acquire.

knowledge from more-advanced countries is more useful when it is new to the industry, when there is a strong interpersonal tie, and when it is easy to access; and knowledge from local sources is more useful when there is a weak interpersonal tie and when it involves a longer conversation.
the usefulness of knowledge from interpersonal ties abroad is influenced by the novelty, accessibility, and discussion duration of the knowledge.

the knowledge that is obtained by individuals from overseas ties is more useful when it is novel and accessible.
the knowledge from more-developing countries is more useful when novel and accessible.

the knowledge of a distant individual is more likely to be useful if the tie between them is strong and they are knowledgeable about the same industry.
